title: Big banks pour billions into India
full_text:
Offshoring The major lenders have quietly set up high-tech hubs, drawn by India's highly skilled workforce and lower wages, writes Jack Derwin.
By rickshaw, the ANZ offices are four minutes away from Commonwealth Bank. Traffic permitting, a prospective employee could be interviewing at National Australia Bank before lunch.
This is Bengaluru, known as the Silicon Valley of India, increasingly a base for Australian banks as they cut costs by sending scores of positions overseas. The capital city of India's southern Karnataka state, is home to more than 1000 support hubs, or as they are more commonly described by their multinational owners, global capability centres.
And Australian banks are appearing increasingly among the global giants, from Microsoft and Nvidia to Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, expanding in Bengaluru. Their local hubs are growing far faster than operations in Australia, and playing an increasingly important role in the technology and back-office support work that underpins lending and deposits.
Filings with the Indian corporate regulator show that ANZ, CBA, NAB and Macquarie paid their local subsidiaries about $1.9 billion in the past year, and directly employed 23,000 staff. The accounts show that the four banks spent another $200 million a year on contractors in India alone.
Previously unreported, the accounts paint a far more detailed picture of the back-office networks that Australia's biggest banks have built offshore.
Most of it has occurred in the past five years.
For the likes of NAB, in the middle of its biggest round of job cuts since 2017, the way it has grown its offshore workforce is partly why it can cut so deeply in Australia, a move that is creating plenty of friction inside the bank.
For the banks and investors, the rationale is clear - the economy is grinding, the housing market is soft, revenue growth is slow and cost are rising. But Angela Robinson, Australian managing director of enterprise technology consultancy Publicis Sapient, says it is also about skills.
"We've traditionally thought about offshoring as moving a role from one geography to another, but that really doesn't describe what's happening here any more," Robinson says. "Yes, there are cost benefits. But primarily, companies are looking to tap into large, highly specialised technology work-forces they can't find anywhere else."
Not long ago, the banks would contract to one of the global technology giants much of this offshore work. Now, they are bringing those jobs in house, more than doubling the number of employees in the past five years.
NAB established its global innovation centre in India in 2022 under then chief executive Ross McEwan and today employs more than 5000 largely permanent workers there. It has another 2000 in Vietnam.
CBA has grown its workforce from almost nothing before the pandemic to nearly 7000 today. It will spend about $250 million in rent and fit-out for a new Bengaluru campus that is slated to open mid next year.
"CBA used to have floors, now it has buildings," says one banker who requests anonymity because of the sensitivity of the plans.
The earliest adopter, however, was ANZ. The Melbourne-based bank has been in India since the 1980s, although its local operations have expanded considerably - both in size and sophistication.
In an interview in 2023, ANZ chief financial officer Farhan Faruqui said there had been a pivot "away from processing to adding value". "And that value is coming in the form of technology and innovation, automation, process improvement, data and insights," he said at the time.
ANZ employs nearly 3000 at its technology arm - known as ANZ Operations and Technology - and another 6100 Indian staff providing support services across the bank. It has another 2000 workers in Manila.
While headcount in ANZ's technology operations has stabilised, staff costs are rising as it hires senior staff for more technical work.
More than one-third of its Indian running costs - some $139 million - still goes to contractors, software and other outside costs, with the bank only recently in advanced discussions with HCLTech and Infosys, according to people briefed on the discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity, as it looks to move software testing to India and cut roles in New Zealand.
Cheaper salaries are a big part of it. At about $31,000 a year, ANZ's back-office employees are paid half the wage of their technology colleagues on the same campus, and a fraction of what Australian staff can expect to take home.
Yet ANZ's spending on its support services hub is also its fastest growing, up 36 per cent to $375 million last year, as the number of employees rises.
Macquarie's another early adopter. It set up its Indian service company in Delhi in 2007, and today its offices in the bustling Gurugram corridor house about 200 staff within walking distance of NAB's second Indian hub.
Macquarie Bank, the entity that owns both Macquarie's Australian banking business and its sprawling global commodities arm, pays for about one-quarter of the centre, according to filings in India. Staff provide finance, accounting, technology, risk management and business operations support.
While it maintains contractors in the country, Macquarie's banking and financial services arm says it has moved full-time jobs back to Australia this year. The broader Macquarie business continued to use India and the Philippines as key hubs supporting its global operations, a spokeswoman said. Macquarie is also expanding with a new Hyderabad office to take care of core technology and "emerging digital domains".
Sri Annaswamy, the founder of outsourcing advisory firm Swamy and Associates, who has advised Australia's big banks on their hubs over the years, says they are treading a well-worn path; bringing in work once done by contractors that can account for as much as one-fifth of their costs, and using newfound scale to build artificial intelligence capabilities.
"CBA in India is no longer hiring data scientists. What they're hiring is predominantly forward deployed engineers, the people who can straight away create, test, and evaluate AI agents," Annaswamy says.
(Westpac is the outlier; it has no global capability centre, although it has thousands of offshore contractors through Genpact and Infosys.)
While ostensibly part of an Australian bank, these Indian subsidiaries are run as separate companies with their own boards, regulatory filings and executives, who are paid hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.
The banks have struggled with turnover in these senior Indian ranks.
CBA has had four senior leaders leave its Indian operations since mid-2024, some lasting just months before being replaced. One managing director was paid about $1.2 million for four-and-a-half months' work before resigning in August last year, according to corporate filings.
ANZ appears to have removed SV Venkataraman, who managed its entire Indian operations, in October 2024, with the subsidiary's accounts noting that its owner had withdrawn his nomination and instructed it to replace him. His successor quit after less than two years in July.
The banks, meanwhile, continue to work to build cultures within their Indian teams. At NAB's grand opening of its new office in Gurugram, many of its top brass flew in to celebrate, including chief executive Andrew Irvine, then chief technology officer Patrick Wright, and then chief operating officer Les Matheson. Updates on the centre's social media pages show frequent events, family days, training opportunities and graduate programs. However, staff are subject to in-country regulations that make it easier and cheaper for banks to hire and fire staff, as technology manager Amit Singhal found after unsuccessfully trying to bring his Indian unfair dismissal case against NAB to Australia's Fair Work Commission in 2024. He has spent the past year pursuing his claim through the Delhi High Court.
While the banks argue that the chase for skills demand these offshore operations, they face the risk of a political and public backlash back home.
NAB's decision to cut 2500 jobs - so soon after it heavily recruited in India and Vietnam - has inflamed tensions between management and staff in the past fortnight. Staff privately point to decisions over the past year, including moving entire technology teams offshore, as evidence the bank has plans to replace employees by stealth. Others say they trained their offshore colleagues knowing they would likely replace them.
It is a burning issue among staff, who at CBA's annual shareholder meeting last month grilled the board on plans to send more jobs to India. "No, we are not planning to increase the number of employees in India," CBA chief executive Matt Comyn said in response to those questions.
Canberra is also watching, in particular the government backbench. One Labor MP, Tom French, told parliament last week that "you cannot make billions from Australians but then treat Australian jobs as expendable".
Another, former industry minister Ed Husic, has foreshadowed that Irvine will face questions on the matter in a parliamentary inquiry next week.
Comyn and ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos should expect questions of their own. AFR
